title: Mobile POS for Bars & Restaurants: Tablets vs. Handhelds
description: Tableside ordering speeds service and lifts order accuracy. Compare tablets and handheld terminals to find the right mobile POS setup for your bar or restaurant.
body:
Every step your servers take between the table and the register is time your guests are waiting. A mobile POS shortens that loop — orders go straight from the table to the kitchen, and checks close where the guest sits. The real question isn't whether to go mobile, but which form factor fits your floor: a tablet, or a dedicated handheld terminal. Both solve the same problem differently, and the right choice depends on how your staff works and where your orders actually happen.

Why Go Mobile in the First Place

Before comparing hardware, it helps to be clear on what you're actually buying. A mobile POS does three things a fixed register can't:

  • Order at the table. Servers enter items the moment a guest asks, so the kitchen sees the ticket while the party is still deciding on drinks refills.
  • Close the check in place. Payment happens at the table, which keeps guests from queuing at a bar or register and frees your host stand.
  • Cut down double-handling. One entry goes straight to the kitchen and the bill, instead of being scribbled, re-keyed, and reconciled later.

The payoff is a smoother shift and fewer mistakes — but only if the device your team carries all night is comfortable and reliable enough that they actually use it.

Tablets: Big Screen, Familiar Feel

A tablet-based mobile POS runs your point-of-sale software on a consumer-style slate, usually mounted on a stand at a counter or carried in a protective case around the floor.

  • Larger, clearer screen. A bigger display means bigger menu buttons, easier modifier selection ("no onions, extra sauce"), and room for photos. That reduces mis-taps and speeds up training for new staff.
  • Familiar to use. Most people already know how to navigate a touchscreen tablet, so the learning curve is short.
  • More flexible. The same device can double as a host-stand register, a self-serve ordering kiosk, or a manager's back-office screen.

The tradeoffs are real, though. Tablets are less durable than purpose-built hardware — a drop on tile is a genuine risk, and a cracked screen can take a station offline mid-rush. They're also bulkier to carry table-to-table, and battery life varies widely depending on the model and how it's being used. If you go this route, invest in a solid case and a stand or mount that keeps the screen at the right angle.

Handhelds: Built for the Floor

A dedicated handheld terminal is designed specifically for hospitality — a compact device with a built-in card reader, a screen tuned for fast order entry, and a body meant to survive drops, grease, and a full shift in someone's hand.

  • Purpose-built durability. Handhelds are made to be carried and bumped. Many are rated to shrug off spills and short drops that would crack a tablet.
  • Faster one-handed entry. Physical buttons or a screen laid out for thumb use let a server ring in an order while balancing a tray in the other hand.
  • Integrated payments. The card reader is built in, so the same device takes the order and the payment without a separate attachment.
  • Longer battery life. Purpose-built terminals are typically sized for a full double shift on a single charge, where a tablet may need a midday top-up.

The downside is cost and flexibility. Handhelds are usually pricier per unit than a tablet, and their smaller screen can feel cramped for long menus with lots of modifiers. They're also single-purpose — you won't repurpose a handheld as a manager's workstation the way you might a tablet.

How to Choose for Your Space

The decision usually comes down to how your floor actually runs, not the spec sheet. Ask these questions:

  • Where does ordering happen? If servers work the table and never leave the floor, a handheld they can hold one-handed wins. If your model is more counter-service or the device stays at a station, a tablet's bigger screen is the better value.
  • How long is a shift? Long, high-volume nights favor a handheld with all-day battery life. A tablet that dies at 9 p.m. is a liability during your busiest hours.
  • What's the menu complexity? Deep menus with heavy customization are easier to navigate on a large screen. Short, fast-turn menus favor speed of entry over screen size.
  • What's your budget? Tablets keep upfront costs lower, especially if you're outfitting several stations. Handhelds cost more per unit but may save you on replacements and downtime over time.
  • What does your POS software support? Not every mobile POS platform runs well on both form factors. Confirm your software is built for the device you're leaning toward before you commit.

Supplies Still Matter on a Mobile Floor

Going mobile doesn't remove the need for the basics — it can make them more important. Handhelds with integrated printers still need the right thermal rolls, and many operators keep a small receipt printer at the bar or host stand as a backup. If your handheld prints from an integrated printer, know which roll size it takes and keep spares where servers can grab them without walking off the floor. A device that runs out of paper at the table is exactly the kind of avoidable stall mobile POS is supposed to eliminate.

Conclusion: Match the Device to How Your Staff Works

There's no universally better option — only the one that fits your floor. If your servers are on their feet all night and want speed and durability, a dedicated handheld is worth the extra cost. If you want a larger, more flexible screen and lower upfront spend, a well-cased tablet gets the job done. Either way, the goal is the same: get orders into the kitchen faster, close checks at the table, and stop making your team walk back and forth to a fixed register.

Your next step: watch one busy shift and note where ordering and payment actually happen, then pick the form factor that matches that reality — and keep the right receipt paper stocked for whatever device you choose.
